claim: Adipocytes increase p53 expression and activity in obesity.
source: It has been known adipocytes increase p53 expression and activity in obesity, however, only canonical p53 functions (i.e. senescence and apoptosis) are attributed to inflammation-associated metabolic phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Only canonical p53 functions (senescence and apoptosis) are attributed to inflammation-associated metabolic phenotypes in obesity.
source: It has been known adipocytes increase p53 expression and activity in obesity, however, only canonical p53 functions (i.e. senescence and apoptosis) are attributed to inflammation-associated metabolic phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: p53 protein expression can be up-regulated in adipocytes by nutrient starvation without activating cell senescence, apoptosis, or a death-related p53 canonical pathway.
source: Here we show p53 protein expression can be up-regulated in adipocytes by nutrient starvation without activating cell senescence, apoptosis, or a death-related p53 canonical pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Inducing the loss of p53 in mature adipocytes significantly reprograms energy metabolism.
source: Inducing the loss of p53 in mature adipocytes significantly reprograms energy metabolism and this effect is primarily mediated through a AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) pathway and a novel downstream transcriptional target, lysosomal acid lipase (LAL).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The effect of p53 loss on energy metabolism in mature adipocytes is primarily mediated through an AMPK pathway.
source: Inducing the loss of p53 in mature adipocytes significantly reprograms energy metabolism and this effect is primarily mediated through a AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) pathway and a novel downstream transcriptional target, lysosomal acid lipase (LAL).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) is a novel downstream transcriptional target of p53.
source: Inducing the loss of p53 in mature adipocytes significantly reprograms energy metabolism and this effect is primarily mediated through a AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) pathway and a novel downstream transcriptional target, lysosomal acid lipase (LAL).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: White adipose tissue (WAT) plays a central role in nutrient homeostasis.
source: White adipose tissue (WAT) plays a central role in nutrient homeostasis, serving as the site of calorie storage and the source of key adipokines (Guilherme et al., 2008; Rosen and Spiegelman, 2006; Kahn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: White adipose tissue serves as the site of calorie storage.
source: White adipose tissue (WAT) plays a central role in nutrient homeostasis, serving as the site of calorie storage and the source of key adipokines (Guilherme et al., 2008; Rosen and Spiegelman, 2006; Kahn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: White adipose tissue is the source of key adipokines.
source: White adipose tissue (WAT) plays a central role in nutrient homeostasis, serving as the site of calorie storage and the source of key adipokines (Guilherme et al., 2008; Rosen and Spiegelman, 2006; Kahn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Obesity is a condition of excess lipid accumulation in white adipose tissue.
source: Obesity is a condition of excess lipid accumulation in white adipose tissue and has been recognized as a major risk factor for many human diseases, including type II diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and some types of cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Obesity has been recognized as a major risk factor for type II diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and some types of cancer.
source: Obesity is a condition of excess lipid accumulation in white adipose tissue and has been recognized as a major risk factor for many human diseases, including type II diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and some types of cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: p53 has been considered a tumor suppressor that can be activated by a variety of stress signals, such as DNA damage, oncogene activation, and other stresses.
source: Traditionally, p53 has been considered a tumor suppressor that can be activated by a variety of stress signals, such as DNA damage, oncogene activation, and other stresses (Vousden and Prives, 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The p53 pathway has downstream effects including cell death, senescence, cell cycle arrest, and autophagy.
source: Once activated, the p53 pathway has a wide range of downstream effects, the most prominent of which are cell death, senescence, cell cycle arrest, and autophagy (Kruiswijk et al., 2015; Maddocks and Vousden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: p53 plays a significant role in metabolic regulation by inhibiting aerobic glycolysis while promoting mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
source: In addition, recent research has shown that p53 plays a significant role in metabolic regulation by inhibiting aerobic glycolysis while promoting mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and that the disruption of p53 function leads to the 'Warburg effect,' which is an enhanced conversion of glucose to lactate in cancer cells (Vousden and Ryan, 2009b; Berkers et al., 2013; Kung and Murphy, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The disruption of p53 function leads to the 'Warburg effect,' which is an enhanced conversion of glucose to lactate in cancer cells.
source: In addition, recent research has shown that p53 plays a significant role in metabolic regulation by inhibiting aerobic glycolysis while promoting mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and that the disruption of p53 function leads to the 'Warburg effect,' which is an enhanced conversion of glucose to lactate in cancer cells (Vousden and Ryan, 2009b; Berkers et al., 2013; Kung and Murphy, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: p53 activation is closely associated with general metabolic regulation.
source: Although most of these studies focused on the malignant transformation of cancer cells, it is clear that p53 activation is closely associated with general metabolic regulation as well (Kung and Murphy, 2016; Krstic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: p53 is involved in normal hepatic glucose homeostasis and lipid metabolism in liver tissue.
source: In addition, several studies have suggested that p53 is involved in normal hepatic glucose homeostasis and lipid metabolism in liver tissue (Prokesch et al., 2017; Derdak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: p53 is important for muscle mitochondrial function.
source: Studies of skeletal muscle also indicate that p53 is important for muscle mitochondrial function (Park et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Studies of adipose tissue have observed increases in the expression and activity of p53 in the adipocytes of obese mice.
source: Studies of adipose tissue have observed increases in the expression and activity of p53 in the adipocytes of obese mice (Yahagi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Adipocyte-specific knockout mice have been generated to study the role of p53 in metabolism.
source: Adipocyte-specific knockout mice (Minamino et al., 2009; Shimizu et al., 2012; Shimizu et al., 2013) have been generated to study the role of p53 in metabolism, but these studies had a number of limitations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: All adipocyte-specific p53 studies have used a system in which p53 ablation was driven by the Fabp4 (fatty-acid-binding protein 4, aP2) promoter.
source: In addition, all adipocyte-specific p53 studies have used a system in which p53 ablation was driven by the Fabp4 (fatty-acid-binding protein 4, aP2) promoter (Fabp4-Cre mice crossed with p53 floxed mice).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about previous studies.

claim: The aP2 promoter has been known to be potentially active in tissues other than adipose, such as macrophages.
source: However, the aP2 promoter has been known to be potentially active in tissues other than adipose, such as macrophages (Fu et al., 2000; Fu et al., 2002; Makowski et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: p53 is known to regulate adipocyte differentiation and fat tissue development in various ways.
source: (iv) Lastly, a lack of attention to adipocyte differentiation affected by p53: p53 is known to regulate adipocyte differentiation and fat tissue development in various ways (Thompson et al., 1998; Inoue et al., 2008; Okita et al., 2014) that may significantly impact energy metabolism when common germline or embryonic p53 knockout mouse models are used.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Adipocytes express the p53 protein under normal conditions in healthy mice.
source: In healthy mice, we observed that adipocytes express the p53 protein under normal conditions and that p53 expression can be significantly up-regulated with 24 hr fasting and down-regulated with refeeding (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: p53 expression in adipocytes can be significantly up-regulated with 24 hr fasting.
source: In healthy mice, we observed that adipocytes express the p53 protein under normal conditions and that p53 expression can be significantly up-regulated with 24 hr fasting and down-regulated with refeeding (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: p53 expression in adipocytes is down-regulated with refeeding after fasting.
source: In healthy mice, we observed that adipocytes express the p53 protein under normal conditions and that p53 expression can be significantly up-regulated with 24 hr fasting and down-regulated with refeeding (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A short-term (3 days) switch from a low-fat to high-fat diet significantly up-regulated the p53 protein abundance in the adipocytes of C57BL/6 mice.
source: We also observed that a short-term (3 days) switch from a low-fat (Research Diet, D1245B) to high-fat diet (HFD) (D12492) significantly up-regulated the p53 protein abundance in the adipocytes of C57BL/6 mice as well (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: p53 can be up-regulated with long-term (12 wks) HFD feeding.
source: In addition, p53 can be up-regulated with long-term (12 wks) HFD feeding (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: p53 pathway downstream genes related to cell senescence, apoptosis, and death (Cdkn1a, Gadd45, and Cdkn2a) were up-regulated by long-term HFD but unaffected by 24 hr fasting and short-term (3 days) HFD feeding.
source: However, the p53 pathway downstream genes traditionally related to cell senescence, apoptosis, and death, such as Cdkn1a, Gadd45, and Cdkn2a, behaved differently. These markers were up-regulated by long-term HFD but unaffected by 24 hr fasting and short-term (3 days) HFD feeding (Figure 1D–E), which suggests the non-canonical function of p53 may be activated under these short-term metabolically challenging conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D-E.

claim: The non-canonical function of p53 may be activated under short-term metabolically challenging conditions.
source: However, the p53 pathway downstream genes traditionally related to cell senescence, apoptosis, and death, such as Cdkn1a, Gadd45, and Cdkn2a, behaved differently. These markers were up-regulated by long-term HFD but unaffected by 24 hr fasting and short-term (3 days) HFD feeding (Figure 1D–E), which suggests the non-canonical function of p53 may be activated under these short-term metabolically challenging conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential behavior of canonical pathway markers under different conditions.

claim: After switching from a normal culture medium to a fasting medium for 6 hr, the p53 expression level in 3T3-L1 adipocytes was significantly up-regulated.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, after switching from a normal culture medium (10% FBS in high-glucose DMEM) to the fasting medium for 6 hr, the p53 expression level was significantly up-regulated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Refeeding (with a normal culture medium with 10 nM insulin) reduced the p53 expression back to a non-fasting condition in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: However, refeeding (with a normal culture medium with 10 nM insulin) reduced the p53 expression back to a non-fasting condition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: p53 up-regulation by fasting in 3T3-L1 adipocytes was not associated with canonical pathway activation in contrast to doxorubicin.
source: Of note, this p53 up-regulation was not associated with canonical pathway activation in contrast to doxorubicin, a DNA replication inhibitor used widely as a p53 pathway activator for cell senescence, cell cycle arrest, and cell death (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Fasting can cause adipocytes to undergo significant reprogramming of cellular energy metabolism.
source: Since fasting can cause adipocytes to undergo significant reprogramming of cellular energy metabolism, these data suggest that p53 may be directly involved in adipocyte metabolic regulation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: p53 may be directly involved in adipocyte metabolic regulation.
source: Since fasting can cause adipocytes to undergo significant reprogramming of cellular energy metabolism, these data suggest that p53 may be directly involved in adipocyte metabolic regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p53 is upregulated during fasting without canonical pathway activation.

claim: p53 affects adipocyte differentiation.
source: Previous research has shown that p53 affects adipocyte differentiation, which could have profound and indirect effects on adipocyte metabolism.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous research.

claim: Glucose concentration in the culture medium of p53-KO adipocytes decreased much more quickly than WT control cells.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, glucose concentration in the culture medium of p53-KO adipocytes decreased much more quickly than WT control cells, indicating that the deletion of p53 can enhance adipocyte glucose consumption.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The deletion of p53 can enhance adipocyte glucose consumption.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, glucose concentration in the culture medium of p53-KO adipocytes decreased much more quickly than WT control cells, indicating that the deletion of p53 can enhance adipocyte glucose consumption.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glucose concentration decreased more quickly in p53-KO cells.

claim: A higher glycolytic capacity and glycolytic reserve were observed in the p53-KO 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: Consistent with these results, a higher glycolytic capacity and glycolytic reserve were observed in the p53-KO 3T3-L1 adipocytes, as indicated by their extracellular acidification rates, which were measured using Seahorse XF technology (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C-D.

claim: p53 deletion led to an increase in NADPH levels in adipocytes.
source: As shown in Figure 2E, p53 deletion led to an increase in NADPH levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The increase in NADPH levels in p53-KO adipocytes did not result from gene expression changes in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD).
source: However, as shown in Figure 2F, these findings did not result from gene expression changes in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) (Jiang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The lactate production of the p53-KO adipocytes was significantly increased, comparing to WT control cells.
source: In the present study, the lactate production of the p53-KO adipocytes was significantly increased, comparing to WT control cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Both the basal and maximum respiration rates were lower in the p53-KO adipocytes than in the WT controls.
source: Both the basal and maximum respiration rates were lower in the p53-KO adipocytes than in the WT controls (Figure 3A), suggesting that mitochondrial function was suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mitochondrial function was suppressed in p53-KO adipocytes.
source: Both the basal and maximum respiration rates were lower in the p53-KO adipocytes than in the WT controls (Figure 3A), suggesting that mitochondrial function was suppressed.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of lower respiration rates.

claim: The p53 knockout adipocytes showed lower ROS levels when compared to the WT cells.
source: When we used Amplex Red to measure the basal cellular ROS levels in the p53-KO adipocytes in vitro, we found that the p53 knockout adipocytes showed lower ROS levels when compared to the WT cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Compared to the WT cells, the p53-KO adipocytes had much higher GSH levels and redox potential.
source: Compared to the WT cells, the p53-KO adipocytes had much higher GSH levels and redox potential (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: p53 plays a key role in promoting mitochondrial respiration and ROS generation in adipocytes.
source: These data suggest that p53 plays a key role in promoting mitochondrial respiration and ROS generation in adipocytes and that deletion of p53 could have the opposite effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p53-KO cells have lower respiration rates and ROS levels.

claim: Deletion of p53 could suppress mitochondrial respiration and ROS generation in adipocytes.
source: These data suggest that p53 plays a key role in promoting mitochondrial respiration and ROS generation in adipocytes and that deletion of p53 could have the opposite effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p53-KO cells have lower respiration rates and ROS levels.

claim: The suppression of mitochondrial function in p53-KO adipocytes was not due to changes in the amount of mitochondria.
source: However, this suppression was not due to changes in the amount of mitochondria, since the copy number of mitochondria was not affected by the p53 (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental data (not shown).

claim: The OCR-to-basal fold change increase was much lower in the p53-KO adipocytes during fatty acid oxidation assays, indicating reduced levels of fatty acid oxidation.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, the OCR-to-basal fold change increase was much lower in the p53-KO adipocytes, indicating reduced levels of fatty acid oxidation, which suggested that fewer free fatty acids were available as energy fuel in the p53-KO adipocytes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Fewer free fatty acids were available as energy fuel in the p53-KO adipocytes.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, the OCR-to-basal fold change increase was much lower in the p53-KO adipocytes, indicating reduced levels of fatty acid oxidation, which suggested that fewer free fatty acids were available as energy fuel in the p53-KO adipocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced fatty acid oxidation.

claim: The long-term (>12 hr) lipolysis rates were significantly decreased in p53 knockout cells compared to WT cells.
source: Although the acute (30 min) isoproterenol stimulated lipolysis rates in the p53 knockout cells were not affected (data not shown) when compared to the WT cells, the long-term (>12 hr) lipolysis rates were significantly decreased (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The change in long-term lipolysis rates in p53 knockout cells was not due to the traditional neutral lipolysis pathway.
source: This change was not due to the traditional neutral lipolysis pathway, since the total protein expression and phosphorylated levels of perilipin and HSL were the same between the p53 knockout and WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: LAL gene expression level was up-regulated in 'fasted' 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, consistent with previous report (Lettieri Barbato et al., 2013), we found LAL gene expression level was up-regulated in 'fasted' (ISO in PBS with 1% BSA) 3T3-L1 adipocyte, and this effect was at least partially dependent on p53.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and a citation to previous literature.

claim: The up-regulation of LAL gene expression in fasted 3T3-L1 adipocytes was at least partially dependent on p53.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, consistent with previous report (Lettieri Barbato et al., 2013), we found LAL gene expression level was up-regulated in 'fasted' (ISO in PBS with 1% BSA) 3T3-L1 adipocyte, and this effect was at least partially dependent on p53.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LAL-RNAi knockdown 3T3-L1 adipocytes impaired ISO-stimulated lipolysis.
source: Furthermore, we also found that LAL-RNAi knockdown 3T3-L1 adipocytes impaired ISO-stimulated lipolysis (Figure 4C–D), suggesting that acid lipolysis was activated after long-term ISO stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-D.

claim: Acid lipolysis was activated after long-term ISO stimulation in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: Furthermore, we also found that LAL-RNAi knockdown 3T3-L1 adipocytes impaired ISO-stimulated lipolysis (Figure 4C–D), suggesting that acid lipolysis was activated after long-term ISO stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LAL knockdown impaired lipolysis.

claim: ATGL RNAi knockdown showed significant downregulation of total lipolysis.
source: In comparison, ATGL (Adipose triglyceride lipase, the enzyme catalyzes the first reaction of neutral lipolysis) RNAi knockdown showed significant downregulation of total lipolysis, and double RNAi knockdowns (LAL and ATGL) further downregulated lipolysis (Fig, 4C-D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-D.

claim: Double RNAi knockdowns (LAL and ATGL) further downregulated lipolysis compared to single knockdowns.
source: In comparison, ATGL (Adipose triglyceride lipase, the enzyme catalyzes the first reaction of neutral lipolysis) RNAi knockdown showed significant downregulation of total lipolysis, and double RNAi knockdowns (LAL and ATGL) further downregulated lipolysis (Fig, 4C-D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-D.

claim: LAL-mediated and neutral lipolysis are the main pathways for lipolysis in adipocytes.
source: These data support LAL-mediated and neutral lipolysis are the main pathways, however, we can't rule out the existence of other lipase that might be involved.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on LAL and ATGL knockdowns.

claim: The overexpression of LAL in p53 null adipocytes completely restored the down-regulation of lipolysis in the p53-KO adipocytes.
source: The overexpression of LAL in p53 null adipocytes completely restored the down-regulation of lipolysis in the p53-KO adipocytes, suggesting that LAL-dependent acid lipolysis is involved (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E-F.

claim: LAL-dependent acid lipolysis is involved in p53-regulated lipolysis.
source: The overexpression of LAL in p53 null adipocytes completely restored the down-regulation of lipolysis in the p53-KO adipocytes, suggesting that LAL-dependent acid lipolysis is involved (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LAL overexpression restored lipolysis in p53-KO cells.

claim: p53-regulated LAL expression is directly involved in lipolysis during nutrient starvation.
source: Overall, these results indicate that p53-regulated LAL expression is directly involved in lipolysis during nutrient starvation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on LAL expression and lipolysis.

claim: p53 binds to the target genes as a tetramer, which comprises two dimers that each binds a decameric half-site with the consensus sequence (p53 response-element, p53-RE, RRRCWWGYYY).
source: It's been known typically, p53 binds to the target genes as a tetramer, which comprises two dimers that each binds a decameric half-site with the consensus sequence (p53 response-element, p53-RE, RRRCWWGYYY, R = A/G, W = A/T, Y = C/T) (El-Deiry et al., 1992; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A highly p53-RE like sequence was found in the LAL promoter region in both mouse and human.
source: When we examined the sequence of LAL promoter region, a highly p53-RE like sequence was found in both mouse and human.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: p53 bound to the p53-RE region in the LAL promoter in fasted mouse adipocytes.
source: By using Chip-qPCR assay we demonstrated p53 bound to this region in fasted mouse adipocytes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: p53-RE deleted construct (Δp53RE) had diminished transcriptional activities even when p53 was over-expressed.
source: Furthermore, by using luciferase reporter assay we show p53-RE deleted construct (Δp53RE) had diminished transcriptional activities even when p53 was over-expressed (Figure 5C–D), supporting that p53 directly regulates LAL gene expression through transcription.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C-D.

claim: p53 directly regulates LAL gene expression through transcription.
source: Furthermore, by using luciferase reporter assay we show p53-RE deleted construct (Δp53RE) had diminished transcriptional activities even when p53 was over-expressed (Figure 5C–D), supporting that p53 directly regulates LAL gene expression through transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of p53-RE diminished transcriptional activity.

claim: Previous studies in non-adipocytes have suggested that glucose starvation causes p53 up-regulation associated with p53 phosphorylation through AMPK-dependent pathways.
source: Previous studies in non-adipocytes have suggested that glucose starvation causes p53 up-regulation associated with p53 phosphorylation through AMPK-dependent pathways (Jones et al., 2005; Feng et al., 2005; Feng et al., 2007; Assaily et al., 2011; Armata et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: p53 was serine/threonine (p-S/T) phosphorylated by nutrient starvation in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: We found that p53 was serine/threonine (p-S/T) phosphorylated by nutrient starvation in 3T3-L1 adipocytes and that refeeding reversed this change (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Refeeding reversed the p53 phosphorylation induced by nutrient starvation in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: We found that p53 was serine/threonine (p-S/T) phosphorylated by nutrient starvation in 3T3-L1 adipocytes and that refeeding reversed this change (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Treatment with the cell-permeable AMPK activator AICAR significantly up-regulated p53 phosphorylation levels.
source: When the cells were treated with the cell-permeable AMPK activator AICAR, the phosphorylation levels were significantly up-regulated (Figure 6B–C), whereas using compound C, an AMPK inhibitor (Zhou et al., 2001), before fasting significantly prevented fasting-induced p53 phosphorylation (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6B-C.

claim: Using compound C, an AMPK inhibitor, before fasting significantly prevented fasting-induced p53 phosphorylation.
source: When the cells were treated with the cell-permeable AMPK activator AICAR, the phosphorylation levels were significantly up-regulated (Figure 6B–C), whereas using compound C, an AMPK inhibitor (Zhou et al., 2001), before fasting significantly prevented fasting-induced p53 phosphorylation (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6B-C and a citation.

claim: Fasting-induced LAL gene up-regulation can be significantly inhibited by AMPK inhibitor, compound C.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, fasting-induced LAL gene up-regulation can be significantly inhibited by AMPK inhibitor, compound C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Metformin is a widely used anti-diabetic drug that has clear benefits in relation to glucose metabolism and diabetes-related complications.
source: Metformin is a widely used anti-diabetic drug that has clear benefits in relation to glucose metabolism and diabetes-related complications (Sivalingam et al., 2014; Foretz et al., 2014), but the mechanisms underlying these pleiotropic benefits are complex and still not fully understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Metformin is believed to act mainly through reducing hepatic glucose production by AMPK activation.
source: Metformin is believed to act mainly through reducing hepatic glucose production by AMPK activation (Zhou et al., 2001; Hundal et al., 2000; Shaw, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mechanism of metformin action has been challenged by studies in AMPK-deficient genetic mouse models, in which metformin effects were still preserved, suggesting an AMPK-independent mechanism.
source: However, this mechanism has been challenged by studies in AMPK-deficient genetic mouse models (Foretz et al., 2010), in which metformin effects were still preserved, suggesting an AMPK-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Metformin can slightly induce p53 phosphorylation, but the effect of 'fasting' was largely impaired.
source: Our data show although metformin can slightly induce p53 phosphorylation, the effect of 'fasting' was largely impaired (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Metformin treatment can increase glycolysis and inhibit lipolysis in adipocytes.
source: Metformin treatment can increase glycolysis, and inhibit lipolysis, however, these effects were not observed in the p53 knockout 3T3-L1 adipocytes (Figure 6F–G), suggesting that metformin acts in a p53-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6F-G.

claim: The effects of metformin on glycolysis and lipolysis were not observed in the p53 knockout 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
source: Metformin treatment can increase glycolysis, and inhibit lipolysis, however, these effects were not observed in the p53 knockout 3T3-L1 adipocytes (Figure 6F–G), suggesting that metformin acts in a p53-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6F-G.

claim: Metformin acts in a p53-dependent manner in adipocytes.
source: Metformin treatment can increase glycolysis, and inhibit lipolysis, however, these effects were not observed in the p53 knockout 3T3-L1 adipocytes (Figure 6F–G), suggesting that metformin acts in a p53-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that metformin effects were absent in p53-KO cells.

claim: When p53-iAKO mice were fed a diet containing doxycycline, the p53 expression in white adipose tissue was significantly reduced, specifically in comparison to the liver tissue.
source: In this model, when the mice were fed a diet containing doxycycline, the p53 expression in white adipose tissue was significantly reduced, specifically in comparison to the liver tissue (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7B-C.

claim: Under normal physiological conditions, no obvious metabolic phenotypes were observed between the WT control and p53-KO mice, including body weight, overnight fasting glucose, and insulin.
source: In these baseline studies, we did not observe any obvious metabolic phenotypes, including body weight, overnight fasting glucose, and insulin, between the WT control and p53-KO mice (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experimental data (not shown).

claim: When challenged with prolonged fasting (24 hr), the body and fat tissue weight losses, fasting glucose and serum-free fatty acid levels, and liver TG content were much lower in the p53-iAKO mice.
source: However, when we challenged the mice with prolonged fasting (24 hr, started from 5 p.m.), we observed that the body and fat tissue weight losses, fasting glucose and serum-free fatty acid levels, and liver TG content were much lower in the p53-iAKO mice (Figure 7E–I), suggesting a potentially attenuated lipolysis ability within adipose tissue.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7E-I.

claim: p53-iAKO mice have a potentially attenuated lipolysis ability within adipose tissue.
source: However, when we challenged the mice with prolonged fasting (24 hr, started from 5 p.m.), we observed that the body and fat tissue weight losses, fasting glucose and serum-free fatty acid levels, and liver TG content were much lower in the p53-iAKO mice (Figure 7E–I), suggesting a potentially attenuated lipolysis ability within adipose tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of lower weight loss and metabolic parameters.

claim: Serum lactate concentration was slightly higher in p53-iAKO mice, but did not reach statistical significance.
source: Serum lactate concentration was slightly higher in p53-iAKO mice, but did not reach statistical significance, and blood pH remained unchanged (Figure 7J–K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7J-K.

claim: Blood pH remained unchanged in p53-iAKO mice compared to WT.
source: Serum lactate concentration was slightly higher in p53-iAKO mice, but did not reach statistical significance, and blood pH remained unchanged (Figure 7J–K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7J-K.

claim: p53-iAKO mice had higher clearance rate for lactate, indicating up-regulated hepatic gluconeogenesis.
